From An Owl
One of the more pleasant tasks of the President of the
Executive Council is to communicate with our undergradu
ates and alumni through the medium ofthe DIAMOND. I
asked for and was granted the privilege ofwriting this column
for each ofthe issues ofthe DIAMOND during my tenure as
President. I hope that, with this new addition, I will have
an
opportunity to share with you the latest developments in
Psi Upsilon as well as our
hopes for the future ofthe Fraterni
ty.
Following/. Russell McShane, Delta '32, as President of
the Executive Council is a task that few should attempt much
less hope to be successful in accomplishing. Brother
McShane's five years of devoted service to the Fraternity as
President, coupled with his many years of service previously
as a member of the Executive Council and as a long-time
Delta Chapter leader, have brought him that rare opportu
nity to spend some time with his wife, Evelyn, and his
family. Do not think for a minute that Russ will not be
attending Executive Council meetings with former Presi
dent Bob Morey in tow, singing in tandem and continuing to
contribute to the development ofthe Fraternity. We are all
grateful to both Russ and Bob for their ongoing willingness to
make available to others the valuable experiences that they
had as Psi U undergraduates "several" years ago and every
year since.
Two events of major significance are occurring during this
academic year. The first is the establishment of an Owl
Club at Brown University after many years of inactivity on
that campus. The Owl Club was officially pledged on Fri
day, May 3, 1985, in Providence, Rhode Island. The under
graduates so pledged at that time are now diligently working
toward reactivation of the Chapter itself by meeting the
requirements ofthe Fraternity's "Guidelines Toward Chap
ter Acceptance," including development of strong ties to the
University, among themselves, and with the alumni of the
Sigma Chapter.
The second event is the momentum that has recently been
generated to reestablish and reactivate our Ep.silon Chapter
at the University of California at Berkeley . The wonderful
initiative and support generated by our Epsilon Chapter
alumni in the Bay Area are a remarkable tribute to their
devotion to seeing a strong Epsilon Chapter return to the
campus. Field Director Pierre Barcik's monumental efforts
to assist in developing the undergraduates there who are
interested in "beginning again" have contributed immeasur
ably to the Fraternity's strong hopes for reestablishing an
important foothold on the West Coast for Psi U.
The rejuvenation oftwo ofour esteemed Chapters is one of
the many goals that the Fraternity has set for itself in recent
years. Recent reactivations ofthe Rho, Nu, Epsilon Phi, and
Chi Chapters have established our
abihty to bring back into
the bonds those Chapters that have long and healthy histo
ries of contribution to the Fraternity. Adding the Sigma and
Epsilon Chapters back into the active Fraternity fold will
bring the Fraternity to a total of 33 active Chapters, more
than we have ever had in our history!
Reestablishing old Chapters and bringing in new Chapters
has not been an easy task. It could never have been accom
plished without the long efforts of our Executive Vice Presi
dent and the two Field Directors who have toiled long and
hard to see these efforts reach fruition. Their efforts would
not have been possible without the continuing and increased
support which so many of you have made possible through
your generous gifts to the Annual Giving Program each year.
We continue to be committed to having two Field Directors
to assist the Executive Vice President in giving direct assist
ance to each of our Chapters every year, not just when an
emergency occurs. Your support to the Annual Giving Pro
gram makes it possible for us to make this vital service
available to each Chapter in a timely and planned fashion.
We are also grateful to the Psi Upsilon Foundation, Inc.,
for its critical assistance in providing both scholarships to our
undergraduate brothers and grants to the Fratemity for the
various educational functions we perform, including Di
visional Conferences, the annual Convention, the Under
graduate Advisory Board and the publication of the DI
AMOND. The Foundation's support for each of these func
tions provides us with the means to better carry out our
mission to provide a meaningful undergraduate learning
experience outside the classroom to our brothers. The retire
ment this spring of Bob McDowell as President of the
Foundation has brought Bob Kaiser, Zeta '39, firmly into the
Foundation as its new President. Bob Kaiser is a long-time
member of the Executive Council and an even longer-time
leader at the Zeta Chapter at Dartmouth. His valuable ex
perience in college fund-raising at Dartmouth will be put to
maximum use in this new
capacity and is greeted with great
enthusiasm by the Fraternity. We know that Bob McDowell
will still be available to lend his wise and helpful advice to the
Foundation and wish to thank him for his devoted service as
President of the Foundation during the past several years.
My purpose in this introductory column was to give you an
overview of a number of measures of progress for the
Fraternity that we are
currently experiencing. I will explore
new avenues with you in future columns. Until then, I am

Executive Council President Steps

But Not Out
After a very successful and highly pro
ductive five-year term, Russ McShane,
Delta '32, stepped down as the sixteenth
president of the Executive Council on
November 15. He is succeeded by Bill
Robie, Epsilon Omega '66, a member of
the Executive Council since 1969 and its
secretary since 1979.
The annual New York Founders' Day
dinner which followed the Executive
Council meeting that day provided a per
fect opportunity to honor and thank
Brother McShane for his years of dedi
cated and faithful service to the Fraterni
ty. Psi U was privileged to have on hand
two other former presidents ofthe Execu
tive Council, both of whose devotion to
and interest in the Fraternity remain as
strong as ever: Jerry Brush, Delta Delta
'39 (thirteenth president) and Bob
Morey, Pi '20 (fifteenth president). They
offered their congratulations to Brother
McShane for his successful tenure as
Psi U's leader and reaffirmed their ded
ication to what they believe is the finest
fratemity in the world. Bob Morey said it
best: "I thank God I'm a Psi U."
Master of Ceremonies Henry Poor,
Gamma '39, introduced Eldred Halsey,
Delta '58, president of the Delta Cor
poration, who spoke of Russ's tireless
work for the Delta for the last fifty-six
years and for the intemational fraternity
for at least twenty years, especially as its
president for the last five. He cited the
long and proud involvement ofthe Delta
Chapter in the Fraternity's governance,
starting with the first president of the
Executive Council, William F. Morgan,
Delta 1865.
It was Andy Lebert, Delta '32, class
mate and lifelong friend of Russ
McShane's, who recounted some of
Russ's personal and professional accom
plishments:
"Fifty-six years ago Russ and I
appeared on the N.Y.U. Heights campus
to begin our academic careers. Shortly
after our arrival in September, 1928, we
were
pledged to the Delta and initiated
later than fall. During our freshman year
Russ participated in many campus and
interfraternity activities, early on demon
strating his athletic capabilities by his
swimming feats as a member of the
N.Y.U. swim team.
"In his sophomore year Russ really be
gan to blossom. He was elected class
president and was considered one of the
leading performers on the swim team.
Russ McShane, Delta '32, admires the
magnificent engraved pyramid pre
sented to him by the Delta at the Novem
ber 15 New York Founders' Day dinner,
which served as a fitting occasion to hon
or him as he stepped down as the 16th
President of the Executive Council.
His ever-increasing participation in cam
pus activities, his performance as a mem
ber ofthe Student Council, and his grow
ing leadership in the Delta and inter
fraternity affairs brought him further rec
ognition from his peers.
"Junior year added to Russ's accom
plishments. He again was elected class
president and a member of the Student

Council. He was respected as the out
standing 50-yard and 100-yard freestyle
swimmer. In addition, his organizing
abilities, dedication, and tireless efforts
continued to be more fully recognized
throughout the campus.
"His undergraduate achievements
reached a
peak in his senior year when he
was elected president of the Student
Council, captain of the swim team, and
president and treasurer of the Delta.
During his term as president ofthe Delta
his leadership was instrumental in de
veloping the Chapter into one which
practiced brotherhood, fellowship, and
loyalty to the fullest. At the end of his
senior year his classmates voted him the
one who had done the most for his college
and the one who had done the most for his
university. The brotherhood voted him
the one who had done the most for the
Delta and Psi Upsilon Fraternity.
"1932, the year we graduated, was not
the ideal year for graduates to seek em
ployment. The Great Depression was at
is lowest point. Russ, with his usual
optimism, did not give up. He was one of
the very few brothers of the Delta who
found employment. His first job was with
McCrory's, a department store chain
which provided him with an opportunity
to observe business in operation.
"In 1933 Russ married Evelyn Reeder,
who had been the girl of his dreams for
many years. Along the way Russ and
Evelyn had three children. Richard, their
firstborn, is now a very successful plastic
surgeon; David is president of McShane
Industries; and Donald is a well-known
financial advisor.
"Being married and having a family
served as an added incentive for Russ to
strive for success in business. His dedica
tion, tireless effort, and his organizing
and sales ability very quickly were recog
nized by the Scott Paper Company. Sub
sequently he became president of C. J.
Wyman Company and then of Baker
Packaging. He ultimately purchased the
Baker Company and served as president
of the Baker-McShane Packaging Com
pany. A few years ago he stepped aside in
favor of his son David. He continues,
however, to be an active participant in
the business.
"Although Russ devoted many hours to
his business career and his family, he
somehow found time for his close friends
and Fraternity brothers. As an alumnus of
the Delta he continued to support and

participate in the activities of the
Fraternity. The success ofthe 1932, 1962,
and 1977 Psi U Conventions hosted by
the Delta were due in large part to Russ's
efforts. He served as a member of the
Delta Corporation and was elected to the
presidency of that group in the 1960s.
"Problems of drugs and the sale of the
Heights campus by N.Y.U. to a commu
nity college necessitated the closing of
the Chapter house on 183rd Street,
which had been a home away from home
for so many of us. Russ McShane stepped
in again, gathered a few brothers
together, and arranged for the sale of the
house, saving as much of the furniture
and archives as he could.
"His strength of purpose and the many
sacrifices he made during that period car
ried the Delta through one of its darkest
hours and gave the Chapter a new lease
on life. In 1975 his rapport with the Uni
versity administration at Washington
Square and his persuasive discussions
with N.Y.U. President Hester provided
the Delta with the house it now occupies
on West 3rd Street. In addition, his
efforts with the administration resulted in
the establishment of other fraternities at
Washington Square.
"Needless to say, when he had suc
ceeded in giving the Delta a second
chance, he saw the need to hold the alum
ni ofthe Heights Colleges together. Russ
had been active in alumni affairs ever
since graduation, and he now saw a new
challenge. He stimulated many alumni
activities and called and wrote many
alumni to raise funds for the University.
He was elected president of the Heights
Alumni Organization and served with dis
tinction. He also continues his activities
to bring the surviving members of the
class of 1932 together each year.
"Much more could be said about Russ's
activities, such as his interest in collecting
bells and his participation in the Bell
Association; his interest in the New
Jersey Sales Executives Association, of
which he once served as president; and
his interest in his church. Throughout his
life Russ has been devoted to his family,
his business, his college, and his fraterni
ty. He has achieved success in all of these
areas. None of his achievements was
given to him. He worked for each and
every one of them by being dedicated,
making sacrifices, maximizing the use of
his inherent ability, and practicing the
basic principles of Psi Upsilon brother
hood �
loyalty and friendship. He is al
ways ready, willing, and able to help
when he is needed."

ble list of contributions to the Fraternity

Russ's term as president ofthe Executive
Council (and vice president before that)
and what, in Andy's opinion, were his two
greatest accomplishments:
1) Overseeing Psi Upsilon's expansion
and reactivation program, which dur
ing the last five years has seen the
birth of three Chapters (Zeta Tau,
Epsilon Iota, and Phi Beta) and the
reactivation of two others (Chi and

force on hazing (chaired by Bill Robie)
and the education of members

DIAMOND articles, etc.
Russ McShane's involvement in the
Fraternity goes even further. For over
thirty years he has taken a leading role in
the New York Metropolitan Association,
spending countless hours organizing
Founders' Day dinners and such. He has
been a director of The Psi Upsilon Foun
dation, Inc. for eight years and, envision
ing great possibilities for the future, was
involved in that body's transition from a
private to a public foundation. And when
the Foundation's Sesquicentennial Fund
Drive was floundering in early 1983, it
was none other than Russ McShane who
stepped in to co-chair it and see it through
its "dark" period.
According to Andy Kerstein, "Every
thing Russ McShane touches in Psi Up
silon turns into golden success. He has
inspired me and so many others to be
come involved in the Fraternity as a
whole, thus insuring an everlasting lega
cy."
Andy Lebert and Eldred Halseyjoined
Andy Kerstein at the podium to present
Russ McShane with a very special and
unique gift from the Delta Chapter, a
magnificent engraved pyramid (to resem
ble a three-sided Delta), designed by
Murray Eskenazi, Lambda '56. On behalf
of the Executive Council, Henry Poor
awarded Brother McShane a beautiful
engraved silver tray, and the Delta
undergraduates bestowed upon him a di
amond-shaped Psi Upsilon plaque.
Russ McShane arrived at the podium to
thunderous applause and laden with gifts.
He thanked the staff and his fellow Ex
ecutive Council members for their assist
ance over the years and reminisced fond
ly about his experiences as president of
the Executive Council. He commented
on the changes which had transpired in
Psi Upsilon during that five-year period
and expressed his unqualified confidence
in Bill Robie to insure the continued
growth of the Fraternity, while at the
same time maintaining the standards of
excellence upon which our beloved
Fratemity was founded.
Brother McShane will continue as a life
member of the Executive Council, and
knowing Russ, his contribution to the
Fraternity will not diminish in the least.

It is with great pride that the Executive
Council welcomed William R. Robie,
Epsilon Omega '66, as its 17th President
on November 15. Bill brings to the office
a wealth of experience and knowledge
about Psi Upsilon and an
absorbing in
terest in the health and welfare of the
Fraternity which began during his days as
an undergraduate at Northwestern Uni
versity and has been sustained and
strengthened over the years.
After being initiated into the Fraterni
ty in 1963, Bill Robie served variously as
Steward, Secretary, and President of his
Chapter. He was the recipient ofthe Out
standing Junior Award and of a schol
arship from The Psi Upsilon Foundation,
Inc. But his list of achievements did not
end with his Fraternity involvement. He
graduated with highest distinction and
departmental honors in political science;
was a member of Phi Beta Kappa, Phi Eta
Sigma, and Deru (senior men's honorary
society); was the University's representa
tive at the West Point Conference on
United States Affairs; was General Chair
man of the 1966 Mock Congress; was
President of the Young Conservative
Club; and was Vice Chairman of the
Young Repubhcan Club.
Brother Robie continued to distinguish
himself at Northwestern University
School of Law. A Dean's List student, he
was Treasurer of the Junior Bar Associa
tion, President of Phi Alpha Delta Law
Fraternity, Treasurer of the Midwest
Federation of College Repubhcan Clubs,
a
participant in the CHICAGO BAR
RECORD Writing Program, and the first
student to sit on the Faculty Admissions
Committee.
Along with the demands and vigors of
law school. Bill Robie assumed the re
sponsibilities of an active member of the
Epsilon Omega Chapter Corporation of
Psi Upsilon. As Chairman of its Building
Fund from 1966-1969, he was largely re
sponsible for raising the necessary funds
to finance construction of a new Chapter
house. In 1969, the Epsilon Omega
hosted the Fraternity's 127th Conven
tion, with none other than Bill Robie as
General Chairman. It is no wonder that,
in the same year, he was elected as one of
the youngest members of the Executive
Council.

member of the Fraternity's administra
tive body, this native of Baltimore, Mary
land has proven himself eminently qualWilliam R. Robie

ified to assume this leadership role. He

ginia area in the early 1970's, he became

the National Capital Interfraternity
Forum in 1976 and served on its Board of
Directors until 1978. His abiding interest
in Psi Upsilon is evidenced by the fact
that he has attended every Convention,
except one, since 1964.
The amount of time and energy Bill
Robie has devoted to Psi Upsilon might
lead one to believe that he has no other
responsibilities in life. Nothing could be
fijrther from the truth! As the Chief Im

dred thirty-six headquarters and field

cating deportation and exclusion cases in
twenty-three base cities and forty detail
locations around the country. Since his
appointment to this position in early
1983, he has successfully developed an
effective and efficient administration of
this system, which has resulted in the
management of a caseload of 68,000 in
1982 growing to 126,000 in 1984.
Bill Robie's association with the United
States Department of Justice dates back
to 1978, during which time he variously
held the positions of Counsel to the
Associate Attorney General, Deputy
Associate Attorney General, Associate
Deputy Attorney General, and Director
ofthe Office of Attorney Personnel Man
agement. He also is an instructor at the
University of Maryland Paralegal Studies
Program and has served as Chairman of
the Paralegal Advisory Board since 1979.
Professional organizations have not suf
fered from a lack ofparticipation and lead
ership from Bill Robie, either. A member

across my desk recently that was a
study
to evaluate the current attitudes of col
lege administrators, campus leaders, and

consumption and abuse to see if any

Results of that study 1 accept as being the
trend. Let's examine some of those find
ings.
1.) To students, drinking is very posi
tively seen as a social facilitator which is a

ness groups like Mothers Against Drunk
en Driving have had little direct impact

dents.

Toward Drinking. The authors con
cluded, and I quote, "Drinking is an ex
tremely important part of the college ex
perience. It is a facilitator that accompa
nies every meaningful social event and is
a sign of a person's well adjusted sociabil
ity. It is normal to drink. Those who don't
drink are the weird ones. It is a way of
establishing yourself socially, creating a
niche for yourself in meeting people,
which is the primary adjustment in com
ing from high school to college. It is a
social learning experience in which
teenagers learn how to handle alcohol,
test their limits, and prepare for later
roles. It is deeply tied to their emerging
masculinity in which they use alcohol to
release tension, lose their inhibitions,
and express pent-up aggressiveness and
sexual frustrations. Most drinking on
campus is viewed as natural or healthy
rebellion. Many students like 'getting
away with it,' drinking without parental

aggerated in the freshman and sopho
more years and tapering off as they be

together.' They expect their drinking to
be even more
responsible and reduced

havior, which they extremely enjoy."
Irresponsible drinking is seen primari
ly as drunkenness, not alcoholism. It is
not ofconcern to students unless it direct
ly affects them. "The halls stink," "I can't
study in the dorm," or "The whole floor
gets assessed for the sink ripped off the
wall,
"
and then more for the incon
venience than because they see it as a
"problem" or "their" problem. "The peo
ple who can't handle it flunk out.
"
So now where do we go after all of this?
We have seen dramatic and important
initiatives taken throughout America. In
every corner, be it the elementary
schoolhouse, college campus, the court
room or in legislatures, both state and
national, new awareness is coming about
concerning the problem of alcohol and
drug abuse. The American college
fraternity movement, long known for its
leadership on important issues in the de
velopment of young men and women,
must step forward once again, take the
gauntlet, and move forward. I challenge
you to assume responsibility for a bold
new approach, attacking this problem

every day, every week, every month and
every year of our lives.

McGiU University
1928
The fall semester at the Epsilon Phi
was an unequaled success. We are proud
to announce that we initiated eleven new
brothers into the bonds in November.
The older brothers are very enthusiastic
about the new initiates and their potential
to lead the Chapter in the years to come.
We look to the winter semester with great
anticipation.
The E Phi was quite active in and
around McGill this semester. As always
our presence was felt on the rugby pitch.
Both the captain and the club president
were Psi U's. The highlight ofthe season
was our ruthless thrashing of all four Har
vard rugby teams. We also have brothers
on the McGill squash and ski teams. The
winter promises to be just as interesting,
as numerous Psi U teams will participate
in the intramural sports schedule.
Each year our
Chapter gets involved in
some sort of community service. This
year we started our charity efforts during
the Christmas season. For two weeks
brothers sold Christmas cards in Mon
treal's Victoria Station. All the proceeds
went to the Grenfell Mission, an orga
nization that sends aid to Labrador fisher
men. Next semester we hope to revive
our Sunday sports events with the chil
dren of the Tyndale-St. George area in
Montreal.
Our relations with our alumni seem to
get better and better with each passing
year. Last year they agreed to finance the
construction of a badly needed basement
bar. We are proud to announce that the
new bar, affectionately known as "The
Blues Bar," is now fiilly operational. It
was quite appropriate that the Zeta Tau's
were here on the evening of our grand
opening, and we thank them sincerely for
donating the first keg to the bar. They
even found it in their hearts to leave us
their prized coffee table, the perfect
touch for the new room.
Our alumni took a major burden off of
our shoulders when they agreed to pay
the remaining amount of our debt to the
International. We were honored to have
Brother David Brown, Epsflon Phi '66,
present at our Founder's Day dinner in
November. It was at this dinner that we
were able to present David, a member of
the International Executive Councfl,
with the check clearing our entire assess
ment balance. We are going to be inten
sifying our efforts to keep in touch with
the alumni because we know that our
Chapter is strong and proud and we
want them to know this as well. Some of
the E Phi's best days he ahead, and we
hope that the alumni will want to get
more involved with us.
The new undergraduate executive is an
excellent group who will undoubtedly
push the Epsflon Phi to new heights. We
are planning once again to embark on
numerous road trips. We feel that these
trips are very worthwhile because they
allow us a unique insight into the various
philosophies that prevail at each Chapter,
besides providing a great time. We
heartily encourage all those Chapters
within our region to seriously consider
visiting one of Psi U's most intriguing
Chapters, located right downtown in
beautiful Montreal.
